name: Data-center shells, land & permits
description_md: Before power and chips comes the right to build: entitled land with water, fiber, and zoning. Developer pipelines are enormous (Vantage alone has a multi-GW global pipeline; the miners-turned-AI and colo REITs add tens of GW more), but local consent is becoming the contested input. Data Center Watch (10a Labs) counts at least 75 US projects worth ~$130B blocked or delayed by opposition in Q1-26 alone — matching all of 2025 in one quarter — with active opposition groups doubling to 833 across 49 states and 300+ state bills introduced; polls show ~71% of Americans oppose data centers near them. The rebuttal, argued by SemiAnalysis: these tallies overweight announcement-stage projects that had no financing, equipment orders, or realistic delivery path — its own 2026 North America capacity forecast moved only ~1%, and hyperscaler self-build (>5GW under construction at the top two alone) proceeds through moratoria via already-entitled land banks. Status basis: judged watch rather than binding — measured near-term capacity impact appears small (per the SemiAnalysis critique), but the opposition trend line (groups, bills, moratoria) is compounding fast enough that permitting could become the binding constraint for post-2028 sites; both readings are recorded per the contested-claims convention.

controlled_by.share_note: Representative wholesale developer: multi-GW entitled land bank across NoVA/Texas/EMEA; land position = the product (company_claimed). Ultimate control sits with county boards, state legislatures, and water/zoning authorities — not tracked as entities

dependents.dependency_md: Leases shells from developers plus self-builds; both routes queue behind entitlement — its paused/reshuffled leases in early 2025-26 showed shell commitments are the first knob turned when plans change.
Multi-GW greenfield campuses (Louisiana, Ohio) depend on local approvals, water agreements, and tax abatements negotiated site by site; Hyperion drew organized water-use opposition.
Gigawatt-campus strategy requires assembling rural land + power + permits at unprecedented scale; each new site is a bespoke political negotiation (Abilene: ~$3.4B local incentives).

substitutes_md: Geographic arbitrage is the main valve: shifting to permit-friendly secondary markets (the documented 'next hotspots' migration out of NoVA/Phoenix), state-level preemption and fast-track statutes, federal land initiatives (DOE sites offered for AI DCs), building in already-industrial zones (brownfields, shuttered factories, mining sites), and international placement (Middle East gigacampuses via Humain/G42). Retrofitting existing shells and powered-land acquisitions (buying entitled-but-unbuilt sites) substitute for new entitlement — at a scarcity premium. None of these relieve water-stressed or moratorium jurisdictions; they route around them.
downcycle_md: Land and shells are where an AI demand fall would be least painful and most visible: options on land expire quietly, announced campuses become 'paused' press releases, and speculative powered-land flippers eat the writedowns. Wholesale developers with signed hyperscaler prelease contracts (typically 10-15-year terms with credit-worthy tenants) are protected; merchant shell builders without anchor tenants are not — the 2001-02 carrier-hotel glut is the analog, when empty colo shells traded at cents on the dollar. A glut would also flip local politics: counties that fought data centers would court them for the tax base. Watch prelease rates on under-construction shells and the spread between entitled-land and raw-land prices as the quality indicators.
